> Neural networks earned their reputation on problems that look nothing like a
> 338-row spreadsheet.

## Learning objectives

1. Describe what a neural network is without mystification.
2. Explain why deep learning needs large datasets.
3. Name the biological problems where it genuinely won, and why.
4. Decide honestly whether your problem qualifies.

## What a neural network is

A stack of linear transformations with non-linear functions between them, fitted
by gradient descent. That is the whole idea. "Deep" means many layers.

The power comes from **learned representations**: you do not hand-engineer
features, the network derives them. That is also the cost — the features it
learns are usually not interpretable.

## Why it needs so much data

Each connection is a parameter. Modern architectures have millions. Fitting
millions of parameters requires enormous numbers of examples, or the network
memorises.

::: {.callout-important}
## The scale mismatch
AlphaFold trained on ~170,000 structures. Nanopore basecallers train on
billions of signal-base pairs. If you have 338 samples, you are five orders of
magnitude away from this regime. **Deep learning is not the tool.**
:::

## Where it genuinely won

| Problem | Why it worked |
|---|---|
| Protein structure | 170k solved structures; clear input/output; objective metric |
| Basecalling | Effectively unlimited training signal |
| Variant effect | Large curated databases |
| Image analysis | Transfers from a field with millions of labelled images |

The pattern: **massive labelled corpora, well-defined objective, tolerance for
opacity.**

## Sequence models

DNA is a string, so architectures from language modelling apply. Transformers
handle long-range dependencies — relevant because regulatory elements act at
distance.

This is genuinely promising, and mostly it means **using pre-trained models**,
not training your own. Fine-tuning an existing model on a few hundred sequences
is occasionally reasonable. Training from scratch on your cohort is not.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pre-trained does not mean unbiased
Genomic models are trained overwhelmingly on European-ancestry data. Applied to
African cohorts, performance can degrade in ways that are silent and
systematic. For Southern African genomics this is not hypothetical — it is a
live problem, and one your work is positioned to document.
:::

## The honest self-assessment

1. Do I have >10,000 labelled examples? If no, stop.
2. Do I need learned features, or do I know the mechanism?
3. Can I tolerate an unexplainable answer?
4. Has my baseline been beaten yet?

Most biological questions in this workshop fail at step 1. That is not a
limitation of your science — it is a property of the method.

## Exercises

1. Estimate the parameter count for a small network. Compare to your sample size.
2. Find a published deep learning genomics paper. What was n? Would it work on
   your cohort?
3. Argue the case *against* deep learning for a problem in your own work.

## Takeaways

- Neural networks are function approximators, not magic.
- The data requirement is the binding constraint.
- Pre-trained models carry their training data's ancestry bias.
